captions.text: Deep in a Florida swamp, tall cypress trees reach for the sky.
Something white hangs in the shade. A ghost orchid!
When an orchid's seed pod splits open, out pour its seeds.
Thousands of them. Each one is as tiny as a speck of dust.
A seed? As tiny as dust?
Zoom in a hundred times. Each seed is a thin, see-through bag.
Fern spores are tiny, too. They drift on the air like dust.
So how can you tell a tiny seed from a spore?

words: A plant part that can grow into a new plant. A seed has a protective coat with a tiny baby plant (embryo) and stored food inside.
A single tiny cell that can grow into a new plant. Most spores are much smaller than a seed.
To sort things into groups based on what they have in common.
To make new living things of the same kind. Every plant reproduces so its kind can keep on living.
Information you observe or measure that supports an explanation. Good scientists use evidence before they decide.
Something that repeats the same way across different examples. Patterns help scientists make predictions.

parts.title: Some Plants Use Spores
parts.html:
Ferns, mosses, and some other plants never make seeds. They reproduce with spores. A spore is just one tiny cell with a thin, tough wall. You often can't see spores without a magnifying glass.

Spores form in small clusters on the underside of fern leaves. The fern releases them, and they drift away on air or water. Most land in the wrong place, so scientists estimate one fern can release millions of spores. A spore that lands somewhere damp first grows into a tiny green heart-shaped plant. A new fern grows from that heart.

parts.title: Some Plants Use Seeds
parts.html:
Many plants reproduce using seeds. A seed is a package. Inside its tough seed coat is a tiny baby plant, called an embryo, and stored food to help it start growing. A small scar, the hilum, shows where the seed was attached to its parent.

Seeds come from flowers, fruits, and cones. A seed that lands in a good spot, with water and warmth, can start to grow.

parts.title: Scientists Classify with Evidence
parts.html:
How do scientists tell seeds and spores apart? They look at the evidence: size, where it came from, and what is inside. Botanists, scientists who study plants, sort plant parts this way.

Sometimes there isn't enough evidence to be sure. Then scientists write "not enough evidence" instead of guessing. That's more honest, and more useful.

compare.title: What makes a seed different from a spore?

curator.A: Baby plant + stored food → seed. A seed carries its own packed lunch, so its baby plant can start growing as soon as it gets water.
curator.B: One tiny cell → spore. A spore is so small it drifts like dust. It has no baby plant inside, so it grows into a tiny heart first.

wall.locked: Brush the layer above first. The elevator goes down, one layer at a time.
wall.first: Brush the glowing top layer. Drag across it (or tap it again and again).
wall.next: Going deeper and older. Brush Layer {n}.
wall.endText: Look at the line. The deepest, oldest fossil is a tiny spore plant. Then come ferns, then cones full of seeds. The flower fossil is in the youngest layer, at the top.
wall.rule: Deeper layers are older. The oldest plant fossils are spore plants. Seeds in cones came later, and flowers came last. Scientists think spore plants grew on land long before seed plants.

wow.title: A 2,000-year-old seed that grew
wow.alt: A young date palm with long, feathery leaves, growing behind a low fence under a blue sky
wow.caption: Methuselah, a date palm grown from an ancient seed · Kibbutz Ketura, Israel
wow.html:
Long ago, people stored dates in a desert fortress in Israel. Scientists found some of the seeds. Tests showed they were about 2,000 years old. In 2005, scientists planted one, and it sprouted!

How? A seed is a package. Its tough coat kept the baby plant safe, and its stored food was still there when the seed finally got water.
wow.insetCap: Date palm seeds, each about as long as a paper clip.

keyIdea: Seeds and spores both help plants reproduce. A seed carries a baby plant and stored food inside a coat. A spore is just one tiny cell, with no baby plant and no stored food. Scientists use size, where it came from, and what's inside as evidence to tell them apart.

quiz.q: A scientist finds fine, powdery dust on the underside of a fern leaf. What is it most likely?

options.t: Spores. Ferns reproduce with tiny, dusty spores, not seeds.
options.ok: 🍃 Exactly. Ferns don't make seeds at all. That dusty powder is spores. Ferns have reproduced this way for hundreds of millions of years.

options.t: Seeds. Ferns keep their seeds on their leaves.
options.miss: Ferns are plants that reproduce with spores, not seeds. Think about where the powder is coming from and how small it is.
Ferns are plants that reproduce with spores, not seeds. Think about where the powder is coming from and how small it is.
